questions.q: Why do we compute the geometric mean for relative errors?
options: Ratios multiply, so the geometric mean treats 0.5 and 2.0 as equal and opposite
It makes every model look better
why: Correct: the geometric mean of 0.5 and 2.0 is 1.
It is not easier. The reason is fairness for ratios.
It does not change who wins; it is a fair average.

questions.q: Model ranks on 4 series are 1, 3, 2, 2. What is the average rank?
Two models tie for the best error on a series (ranks 1 and 2 are tied). What rank does each get with the average method?
questions.why: Both share ranks 1 and 2, so each gets (1 + 2) / 2 = 1.5.

questions.q: The DM test uses which quantity per time step?
options: The loss of the better model
The difference of the losses of the two models
The sum of the actual values
why: One loss is not enough to compare two models.
The actual values alone say nothing about a difference.

questions.q: You tested 40 model variants on the same test set and report the best score. What is the problem?
options: Nothing, the best model is the best
Winner's curse: the best score is optimistic because of selection
why: The best of many noisy scores is biased upwards.
Correct: use a final untouched period to get an honest score.
More models make the selection bias worse.

questions.q: A new model wins on average, but on 3 of 10 series its error is 60% higher than naive. What do you do before you replace the old model?
options: Replace it because the average is better
Investigate those series: size, intermittent demand, new items; maybe use a fallback rule
Delete the 3 series from the test
why: The average hides bad cases that may be important to the business.
Correct: look at the losers, find the cause, and consider a fallback or a different model for them.
Removing hard cases is an unfair comparison.

questions.q: Relative MAE vs naive on three series: 0.5, 1.0, 2.0. What is the geometric mean?
questions.why: The product is 1.0, the cube root of 1 is 1. The arithmetic mean would be 1.17 and look worse.
